meta.title: Who really said "You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Fuller’s idea, but not Fuller’s words. The famous version first appears in Daniel Quinn’s 1999 book, uncited; Fuller’s documented line is different.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete'?
meta.ogDescription: The innovation-deck classic is a paraphrase. Fuller’s recorded words: “you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology.”

answer.label: Fuller’s thought — but not Fuller’s words
answer.sourceLine: Fuller did say something very like this, and there is a transcript: in an interview with the consultant Mike Vance, published in Think Out of the Box (1995), he says “You never change anything by fighting it; you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology” — and then illustrates it with Telstar replacing 500 tons of transoceanic cable. The polished sentence in circulation today is not in that transcript or anywhere else in his work. Its first known appearance is Daniel Quinn’s Beyond Civilization in 1999, sixteen years after Fuller’s death, printed with no source at all.
answer.confidenceText: The idea is documented. This particular sentence is not.

source.excerpt: Bucky sat in a comfortable reclining chair, sipping thoughtfully from his tea cup, as we conducted an unforgettable interview with one of the world’s most unusual people … He spoke quietly: “You never change anything by fighting it; you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology. Telstar replaced 500 tons of transoceanic cable. It used to take us three years to circumnavigate the globe in a wooden-hulled ship. It took three months in a steel ship, 90 minutes in a space capsule and now instantaneously with telecommunications.”
trail: The documented wording and the drift are both laid out by Quote Investigator ↗, whose conclusion is that the Vance interview excerpt in Think Out of the Box (1995) “is probably the most reliable” version, and that “other versions of this quotation do not have solid supporting evidence.”

The earliest printing of the famous wording is Daniel Quinn’s Beyond Civilization, page 137, over Fuller’s name and with no citation. We confirmed the edition — Harmony Books, New York, 1999 — against the Internet Archive’s catalogue record ↗.
The transcript edition checks out too: Think Out of the Box ↗ by Mike Vance, Career Press, 1995 — matching the page-138 citation for Fuller’s recorded sentence.
An independent check agrees: Wikiquote ↗ carries the popular wording but sources it to Quinn’s 1999 book — not to anything Fuller wrote or is recorded as saying.
source.excerptNote: Compare the two carefully. Fuller’s recorded sentence is about superior technology making things obsolete, and he immediately grounds it in hardware. The popular version replaces technology with “build a new model” — a broader, vaguer claim that suits a strategy slide better than it suits an engineer.

author.name: R. Buckminster Fuller
author.heading: About R. Buckminster Fuller
author.bio: Richard Buckminster Fuller Jr. — “Bucky” to almost everyone — was an American architect, inventor, systems theorist and futurist who published more than thirty books and coined or popularised Spaceship Earth, Dymaxion, ephemeralization, synergetics and tensegrity. His best-known invention is the geodesic dome. His central argument, that doing more with less is how real change happens, is exactly the thought this quotation compresses — which is why the paraphrase has been so hard to dislodge.

copyAttribution: The wording everyone quotes — “You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.” — is first documented in Daniel Quinn's Beyond Civilization (1999), p. 137, with no source given. What Buckminster Fuller is documented as actually saying, in an interview transcript published in Think Out of the Box (1995), p. 138, is: “You never change anything by fighting it; you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology.”

misattribution.heading: Right person, wrong words
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the thought really is Fuller’s. What drifted is the sentence, and it drifted through identifiable hands.

items.why: Quinn printed “You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete” over Fuller’s name on page 137 ↗ with no supporting citation. The 2006 Reader’s Digest Treasury of Wit & Wisdom and Kate Raworth’s 2017 Doughnut Economics both carry this exact wording. Quote Investigator also records a looser variant in a 1998 newspaper column, a year before Quinn.

items.tag: The transcript — this one is real
items.why: Their 1995 Think Out of the Box ↗ prints what reads as an interview transcript, which Quote Investigator ↗ judges “probably the most reliable version”. The same book gives a looser epigraph variant on page 78.

The Reader’s Digest Treasury of Wit & Wisdom (2006) carried Quinn’s wording over Fuller’s name, and Kate Raworth opened Doughnut Economics (2017) with it as something “Buckminster Fuller once said” — the route by which it became a fixture of innovation talks.

Eleven years before Quinn, the Tallahassee Democrat reported Vance presenting the idea as “Superior methodology changes more things than fighting and struggling” — attributed to Fuller but, as Quote Investigator notes, not offered as a direct quotation.

misattribution.truthLine: Fuller’s own recorded sentence is “You never change anything by fighting it; you change things by making them obsolete through superior technology” — and he said it about Telstar and transoceanic cable, not about business models. Wikiquote ↗ reaches the same verdict, sourcing the popular version to Quinn’s 1999 book rather than to Fuller.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: This is probably the most-shared sentence attached to Fuller’s name, and it has become shorthand for a whole theory of change: don’t argue with the incumbent, out-build it. Read beside what he actually said, the paraphrase has been quietly broadened. Fuller claimed something narrower and more falsifiable — that superior technology makes systems obsolete — and he kept pointing at machines to prove it.

That matters because the paraphrase is usually deployed as strategy advice, where “build a new model” can mean almost anything. Fuller’s version came with a bill of materials: Telstar against 500 tons of cable, three years round the globe by sail against ninety minutes by capsule.
detailsBody: Mike Vance was a business consultant who had worked at Walt Disney Productions on ideas for Walt Disney World, and he interviewed creative thinkers for material. He described meeting Fuller at a small beach motel in Santa Monica — tea cup, reclining chair — and the interview necessarily happened before Fuller died on 1 July 1983. The transcript was not published until 1995, twelve years later, which is part of why the looser version got ahead of it.

Quote Investigator’s conclusion is deliberately modest and worth keeping whole: the Vance excerpt “is probably the most reliable”, “other versions of this quotation do not have solid supporting evidence”, and — the honest caveat — “Fuller may have expressed this notion in more than one way on different occasions.” So this page says the famous wording is undocumented, not that Fuller could never have said anything like it.
context.pull: He said superior technology. The internet decided he said business models.
